What this notebook is for

There is no ACF work here. This notebook is pure aggregation and time plots: hourly Beijing pollution taken up to weekly and monthly, and weekly fuel prices taken up to quarterly.

Treat it as the setup step that the correlogram depends on. A lag is one step of whatever your index happens to be, so one year back is lag 8760 in hourly data, lag 52 in weekly data and lag 12 in monthly data. index_by() plus summarise() changes that unit, and with it the lag you should be looking at, the length \(T\) of the series, and therefore the white-noise bounds. Choose the resolution before you reach for the ACF, not after.

1. Beijing pollution

The code below imports hourly readings from an air-quality station in Beijing. The station records particulate matter (PM2.5, PM10) and gaseous pollutants (SO2, NO2, CO, O3), alongside basic weather variables. The file Beijing_Pollution_TSeries.csv is in the data/ folder at the repository root:

pollution <- 
  
  # Read the file
  read_csv("../../data/Beijing_Pollution_TSeries.csv") |> 

  #Step 1: create the time_stamp
  mutate(time_stamp = make_datetime(year, month, day, hour)) |>
  
  #Step 2: reorder columns and drop timestamp components (keep only the newly created timestamp)
  select(time_stamp, everything(), -c(No, year, month, day, hour))  |>

  #Step 3: convert to tsibble
  as_tsibble(index = time_stamp)
  
pollution

The code below plots the NO2 readings contained in the dataset:

autoplot(pollution, NO2)

1.1 Average weekly values

Use index_by() to define a new tsibble NO2_weekly that aggregates the hourly values in the tsibble pollution into average weekly NO2 levels. For details on how to use index_by(), refer to the tsibbles notebook from Session 3.

Then add a new column to NO2_weekly that holds the combination of year and month for each row.

Finally, filter the dataset to keep only values between March 2013 (included) and March 2014 (excluded).

2. Fuel Prices

The code below turns the data in the file Weekly Fuel Prices.xlsx into a tsibble. The file is in the data/ folder at the repository root:

fuel_prices <- 
  
  # Read excel file
  read_xlsx("../../data/Weekly Fuel Prices.xlsx",
            col_types = c ("date", "numeric", "numeric")) |> 
  
  filter(!is.na(Date)) |>
  
  pivot_longer(cols = c("Petrol (USD)", "Diesel (USD)"),
               names_to = "fuel_type",
               values_to = "price_USD"
               ) |> 
  
  as_tsibble(key =  fuel_type, regular = FALSE, index = Date)

fuel_prices

2.1 Quarterly aggregation with index_by

The code below produces the average quarterly prices, separated by fuel_type.

Run it with and without the group_by(fuel_type) line that precedes index_by(yq = yearquarter(Date)). How does the result change? Drop it and petrol and diesel are averaged together into a single meaningless series — a silent wrong answer that no warning will catch for you.

For the next section, keep the group_by() and store the result in fuel_quarterly.

fuel_quarterly <- 
  
  fuel_prices |> 
  
  # Use group_by so that the subsequent index_by is applied
  # group-wise.
  group_by(fuel_type) |>

  # Index by yearquarter 
  index_by(yq = yearquarter(Date)) |> 
  
  # Summarise
  summarise(
      # One mean per fuel_type per quarter, so the name must not say "petrol"
      mean_price_USD = mean(price_USD, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |> 

  ungroup()

Filter the object fuel_quarterly to contain only the years 2004 to 2008 (both included).
